tip: Toast the cumin in a dry pan for thirty seconds before it goes in — ground cumin straight from the jar tastes dusty here.

name: Falooda, Blended
tip: Falooda is built on basil seeds and vermicelli; chia is the closest stand-in, so add it last and let the cup sit two minutes before drinking.

name: Thandai Cooler
tip: Soak the almonds in hot water for ten minutes and the blade will turn them to cream instead of grit.

name: Masala Chai Date Shake
tip: Tear the dates open and check for pits, then soak them in the warm concentrate — cold dates ride around the blade in lumps.

name: Aam Panna Cooler
tip: The original uses boiled raw green mango; pick the firmest, least ripe fruit you can find so the drink stays sour rather than sweet.

name: Rose Pistachio Kulfi Shake
tip: Blend the pistachios with the milk alone for ten seconds first — once ice is in the cup the nuts never break down.

name: Solkadhi-Style Coconut Cooler
tip: Solkadhi gets its pink sourness from kokum, which is hard to find — cranberry hits the same sour-and-pink note without pretending to be the same fruit.

name: Horchata, Blended
tip: Real horchata means soaking raw rice overnight and straining it; rice milk with cinnamon gets you most of the way in three minutes.

name: Agua de Pepino con Limón
tip: Peel half the cucumber and leave the rest — all skin turns it bitter, no skin and you lose the green flavour.

name: Agua de Jamaica
tip: Steep the hibiscus twice as strong as you would drink it — the ice in the cup is going to dilute it by half.

name: Horchata de Ajonjolí
tip: Toast the sesame until it starts popping and smells nutty; raw seeds make this taste like wet paper.

name: Tamarind-Style Sour Cooler
tip: This is not agua de tamarindo — prune and lime build the same dark sweet-sour shape, and the pinch of salt is what makes it read as tamarind at all.

name: Jícama con Limón
tip: Jicama skin is fibrous and will not break down — peel it thickly with a knife rather than a vegetable peeler.

name: Agua de Tuna
tip: Buy prickly pears already de-spined, and keep the blend short — the seeds stay whole and pleasant if you don't pulverise them.

name: Tepache-Style Pineapple Freeze
tip: Tepache ferments for days on pineapple rind; kombucha lends the same tang and fizz so you can drink it today.

name: Açaí na Tigela, Drinkable
tip: In Brazil this is a bowl you eat with a spoon and granola on top; blending the granola in thickens it instead, so leave a spoonful for the surface.

name: Limonada Suíça
tip: The whole lime goes in, peel and all, but blend it for seconds only — the pith turns the drink bitter fast.

name: Chicha Morada-Style Cooler
tip: Purple corn is what makes the real thing; black currants give the same deep colour and tannic edge, which is the closest honest substitute.

name: Maracuyá en Leche
tip: Passion fruit is acidic enough to curdle milk if it sits — blend it and drink it, don't make it ahead.

name: Avena Colombiana
tip: Soak the oats in the milk for five minutes first; they blend smooth instead of leaving flecks.

name: Mote con Huesillo, Blended
tip: The Chilean original is whole dried peaches and husked wheat sitting in syrup — dried apricot and cooked quinoa are the stand-ins that blend.

name: Camu Camu Limeade
tip: Camu camu is startlingly sour for a powder — a teaspoon is already assertive, so taste before you reach for more.

name: Halo-Halo, Blended
tip: Halo-halo is layers you stir at the table, and blending trades those layers for something you can drink — a fair swap, but not the same dessert.

name: Ube-Style Purple Shake
tip: There is no ube here — dragon fruit borrows the colour only, so call it what it is rather than serving it as ube.

name: Cha Yen, Blended
tip: Brew the tea at double strength and chill it first — warm tea melts the ice and you end up with beige milk.

name: Pandan-Style Coconut Freeze
tip: Pandan isn't in the pantry; the matcha is here for the grassy colour and a little bitterness, not to imitate the leaf.

name: Es Teler, Blended
tip: Young coconut meat is soft and blends away; mature coconut stays chewy, so buy the frozen young kind if you can.

name: Cendol-Style Palm Sugar Freeze
tip: The green rice-flour worms cannot survive a blender, so this is the other half of cendol: coconut milk and dark palm sugar with salt.

name: Sinh Tố Mãng Cầu
tip: Soursop seeds are hard and bitter — pick every one out by hand before blending, they do not break down.

name: Chanh Muối, Blended
tip: The real version uses limes salted in a jar for months; fresh lime with salt is the quick approximation, and it wants more salt than feels reasonable.

name: Matcha and White Peach
tip: Stir the matcha into a splash of the milk with a spoon before anything else goes in, or it clumps against the frozen fruit.

name: Amazake-Style Rice Cooler
tip: Amazake gets its sweetness from koji fermenting overnight; this borrows the rice body and grated ginger finish, not the fermentation.

name: Misugaru-Style Grain Shake
tip: Misugaru is a roasted multigrain powder — toast the oats, sesame and almonds in a dry pan first and you get much closer to it.

name: Sujeonggwa-Style Persimmon Punch
tip: Sujeonggwa uses dried persimmon softened in spiced syrup; a very ripe hachiya, soft to the point of collapse, is the fresh-fruit route.

name: Lychee Green Tea Freeze
tip: Tinned lychees work and save you ten minutes of peeling — drop the honey to a teaspoon if you use them, they come packed in syrup.

name: Papaya Milk, Taiwanese Style
tip: Blend it briefly and drink it straight away — papaya enzymes turn milk bitter within about ten minutes.

name: Melon Cream Soda Float
tip: Soda foams violently under the blade — pour it in last and run the blender only a few seconds.

name: Black Sesame Soy Milk
tip: Black sesame if you can get it, and toast it until it pops — untoasted seeds give you colour without the roasted flavour that carries this drink.

name: Mango Pomelo Sago-Style
tip: Pomelo is milder than grapefruit, so strip every bit of white membrane off the segments or the bitterness takes over.

name: Goji and Red Date Cooler
tip: Soak the goji berries in the hot tea for five minutes — dry ones stay leathery and leave shreds in the drink.

name: Morir Soñando
tip: Both the juice and the milk have to be properly cold before they meet, or the acid curdles the milk into threads.

name: Guayaba y Queso
tip: Guava seeds are gritty and survive blending — scoop the seedy centres out and use the flesh around them.

name: Irish Moss Drink
tip: Sea moss gel keeps thickening in the cup, so drink this within a few minutes or it sets into something closer to pudding.

name: Doogh-Style Cooler
tip: Add the sparkling water last and blend for three seconds — any longer and you have flat salty yogurt.

name: Tahini and Molasses Shake
tip: Tahini stirred into grape or date molasses is a Levantine breakfast spread — this is that, drinkable, and it wants the molasses to stay assertive.

name: Pistachio Halva Shake
tip: The salt is not optional — halva is sweet enough to go flat without it.

name: Sahlab-Style Freeze
tip: Sahlab is a hot winter drink thickened with orchid-root flour; cold and unthickened, this keeps the rose-and-cinnamon flavour and drops the texture.

name: Laban with Cucumber and Mint
tip: Labneh is thick enough to stall the blade on its own — the water goes in first, then everything else on top.

name: Sekanjabin Cucumber Cooler
tip: Sekanjabin is a honey-and-vinegar syrup, and the balance is personal — start with half the vinegar and add the rest by taste.

name: Sharbat-e Rivas
tip: Raw rhubarb is harsh and squeaky — toss it with the sugar and let it sit five minutes before blending so it softens and gives up juice.

name: Qamar al-Din Apricot Cooler
tip: The proper version starts with sheets of apricot paste soaked for hours; dried apricots in hot water for ten minutes is the weeknight route.

name: Moroccan Avocado Milk
tip: Orange blossom water is strong — a teaspoon perfumes the whole cup, and a tablespoon makes it taste like soap.

name: Şalgam-Style Savoury Cooler
tip: Turkish şalgam is fermented purple carrot and turnip, sour and salty rather than sweet; beet juice and pickle brine get you the same territory.

name: Leche Merengada
tip: Use pasteurised whites from a carton, and blend long enough to foam — the froth is the whole character of the drink.

name: Baobab and Mango Cooler
tip: Baobab powder is tart and chalky and will float in clumps — shake it into the water first, then add the fruit.

name: Zobo-Style Hibiscus Freeze
tip: Zobo is usually brewed with pineapple rind and ginger together; using the fruit itself makes it sweeter, so ease off the sugar.

name: Spris, Blended
tip: In Ethiopian juice houses spris comes layered in stripes and you eat it with a spoon — one cup and one blade means you get the flavours without the stripes.

name: Granita di Limone
tip: A real granita is scraped from a tray over two hours; a cup packed with ice on CRUSH is the shortcut, and it wants more sugar than you'd think because cold mutes sweetness.

name: Granita di Mandorla
tip: In Sicily this is breakfast, eaten with a brioche dunked into it; the extract is powerful, so a quarter teaspoon is the whole dose.

name: Uzvar-Style Dried Fruit Freeze
tip: Uzvar is dried fruit simmered and left overnight; soak the prunes and apricots in hot water for ten minutes and you get a usable version of the same smoky sweetness.

name: Pear Over Oats
tip: Add the chia last and give it two minutes before you blend, or it clumps on the blade.

name: Cocoa and Prune
tip: Prunes and cocoa are both dark and slightly bitter, so they hide each other — this tastes far more like chocolate than like prunes.

name: Spoon-Thick Berry
tip: Psyllium keeps thickening in the cup, so drink this within five minutes or you'll be eating it with a spoon.

name: Fig and Bran
tip: Snip the stems off the dried figs first — they never break down and you'll find them in the last mouthful.

name: Blackberry Seeds and All
tip: Allulose instead of honey keeps the sugar down without the cooling aftertaste erythritol leaves.

name: Four O'Clock Filler
tip: Soluble fibre powder goes cloudy but shouldn't go lumpy — pour it onto the water before the ice, not after.

name: Cold Cucumber Line
tip: Leave the cucumber skin on for colour, but peel it if it's a thick-skinned waxed one — that skin turns bitter under the blade.

name: Fennel and Ice
tip: Use the white bulb only and slice it thin across the grain; the stalks are all string.

name: Tomato, Cold and Salted
tip: The olive oil isn't optional — without a little fat the tomato tastes thin and metallic.

name: Cauliflower Cocoa
tip: Frozen riced cauliflower is flavourless and gives you milkshake thickness for almost no sugar — but it has to be frozen, not fresh.

name: Jicama Lime Ice
tip: Jicama is fibrous, so cut it into half-inch cubes rather than sticks or the blade just pushes them around.

name: A Lot of Cold Watermelon
tip: Freeze watermelon cubes on a tray, not in a bag, or they weld into one block you can't get into the cup.

name: A Pint of Strawberry
tip: Stevia goes bitter if you overshoot, so measure it rather than shaking it in.

name: Cold Pumpkin Cup
tip: Check the can says pumpkin puree and not pie filling — the filling is already loaded with sugar.

name: After the Heat
tip: A quarter teaspoon of salt in coconut water disappears completely — you read it as the lime tasting rounder.

name: Orange Freeze for a Hot Day
Salted Pineapple Cooler
tip: Salt on pineapple is a street-cart trick — it makes the fruit taste sweeter without adding sugar.

name: Spinach Meets Citrus
tip: Vitamin C genuinely improves how much of the iron in leaves your body takes up, so keep the citrus and the spinach in the same glass rather than the same day.

name: Beet Greens and Grapefruit
tip: Beet greens are the part people bin — strip them off the stems and they blend softer than kale.

name: Chard and Kiwi
tip: Tear the chard leaf away from the coloured rib; the rib is where the earthy, slightly salty taste lives.

name: Watercress and Clementine
tip: Watercress is peppery in a horseradish way — start with half a cup if you've never blended it.

name: Kale, Pepper and Lime
tip: Raw red pepper carries more vitamin C than an orange does, and its sweetness sits under the kale instead of fighting it.

name: Tahini and Date
tip: Stir the tahini jar right down to the bottom first — the solids at the base are where the flavour is.

name: Collards and Almond
tip: Collards are tougher than spinach, so run BLEND twice with a shake in between rather than once for longer.

name: Orange Chia Cold Cup
tip: Buy the fortified soy milk if you're drinking this for the calcium — unfortified plant milks have almost none.

name: Fig, Almond, Sesame
tip: Toast the sesame in a dry pan for a minute before it goes in and the whole drink turns nutty instead of raw.

name: Bok Choy and Pear
tip: Use the pale stems as well as the leaves — they're crisp and watery and blend almost to nothing.

name: Walnut and Black Currant
tip: Black currants are properly sour; if yours are frozen and unsweetened you'll want the full teaspoon of maple.

name: Hemp and Cacao
tip: Nibs stay crunchy no matter how long you blend — add them at the end if you want the texture, at the start if you don't.

name: Flax Oil Blueberry
tip: Keep flaxseed oil in the fridge and never near heat — it goes rancid and fishy faster than any other oil on the shelf.

name: Warm-Up Cup
tip: Creatine never fully dissolves — drink it straight away and rinse the cup, or you'll find grit welded to the bottom.

name: Arugula and Beet
tip: Use pre-cooked vacuum-packed beets; raw beet never breaks down properly in a single-serve cup.

name: Cold Apple and Chamomile
tip: Brew the chamomile double strength and chill it first; hot tea poured over ice just gives you weak tea.

name: Cold Broth Cup
tip: Miso goes harsh if you cook it, so this stays cold on purpose — silken tofu makes it thick enough to feel like food.

name: Flat Ginger Ale and Pear
tip: Let the ginger ale go flat in an open glass first — carbonation in a sealed blending cup builds pressure you don't want.

name: Turmeric with the Pepper In
tip: Turmeric on its own is bitter and dusty; the pepper and the coconut fat are what turn it into something you'd finish.

name: Sharp Ginger Cold Cup
tip: Scrape ginger skin off with the edge of a teaspoon rather than peeling it — you lose far less of the root.

name: Cardamom Oat Chai
tip: Extra cardamom on top of a chai concentrate is what stops it tasting like a syrup — most concentrates are heavy on cinnamon and light on everything else.

name: Cinnamon Sweet Potato
tip: Roast the sweet potato rather than boiling it — boiled, it goes watery and the drink tastes of nothing.

name: Carrot with Garam Masala
tip: Garam masala is a finishing spice, so half a teaspoon is plenty — any more and it tastes like uncooked curry powder.

name: Kiwi, Ginger, Nothing Else
tip: Blend kiwi seeds briefly — hammer them and they release a bitterness that wasn't there a moment ago.

name: Greens Powder, Made Drinkable
tip: Greens powder tastes like a lawn in water — pineapple's acid and the banana's sweetness are what make it drinkable.

name: Blue-Green Mango
tip: Half a teaspoon of spirulina colours the whole cup; a full one and you'll taste pond.

name: Sea Moss and Mango
tip: Sea moss gel is essentially a thickener — leave this standing twenty minutes and it sets into a loose pudding.

name: Maca Malt
tip: Maca is malty and slightly bitter, closer to Ovaltine than to vanilla — start at a teaspoon and work up.

name: Ashwagandha and Date
tip: Ashwagandha tastes bitter and faintly horsey on its own; dates and cardamom are the cheapest way to cover it.

name: Reishi Cacao
tip: Reishi is properly bitter, so pair it with Dutch-process cocoa rather than natural — the Dutch stuff is mellower and meets it halfway.

name: Collagen in the Cold Brew
tip: Collagen peptides are flavourless but they foam — blend on the short side and let the head settle before you drink.
